title: Tenant priority shedding and SLA enforcement: architecture notes
content:
TL;DR
This note captures a proposed approach for tenant/org-aware routing that enforces contract SLAs, protects against noisy neighbors, and provides graceful degradation across multi-region deployments. The core idea: map contract-tier -> routing policy -> runtime admission controls + control-plane signals. Implement fast-path shedding in the runtime and use the control plane for longer-term corrective actions and telemetry-driven adjustments.

Goals
- Ensure customers with higher tier/contract commitments get prioritized throughput & latency SLOs.
- Prevent a single tenant (or small group) from degrading cluster-level SLOs for others.
- Make shedding/quotas predictable and explainable to customers.
- Support coherent behavior across regions (local enforcement, global reconciliation).
- Keep operational surface small: simple primitives in runtime + flexible policies in control plane.

Assumptions and constraints
- We have per-tenant metadata (tier, committed qps, contract SLA, region affinity) available in the control plane and exposed to the routing layer via a fast cache (ttl ~30s).
- Serving runtime can make O(1) decisions per request with small memory and CPU overhead.
- We cannot rely on synchronized global token buckets for tight latency SLOs; prefer local counters + periodic reconciliation.

Threat model / failure modes
- Sudden traffic spikes from a tenant (noisy neighbor) causing increased queueing and token latency.
- Slow region due to degraded infra causing cascading retries.
- Misconfigured tier on an account allowing higher priority than contracted.
- Control plane outage (must default to safe, conservative behavior).

Core concepts and primitives
1) Priority tiers (immutable per-tenant, set in contract): platinum, gold, standard, trial. Tiers map to numeric priority weights (e.g., 100, 50, 20, 5).
2) Local capacity pool: each serving node has a view of available concurrency / token capacity expressed as a soft budget and hard limit.
3) Admission control points: at the API gateway (ingress) and at the runtime worker scheduler. Fast decisions must be made at ingress to avoid wasted work.
4) Token buckets for throughput shaping: small local buckets per-tenant per-node for short-term smoothing (100ms-5s windows); acknowledgement and refill controlled locally.
5) Circuit breaker / backoff: per-tenant state that protects cluster health; trips when error rates or queue latency cross thresholds.
6) Fallback routing: compatibility mapping to cheaper model variants or degraded feature set for non-critical tiers.
7) Control-plane policy engine: stores SLA mappings, global quotas, and can evict, throttle, or migrate tenants based on longer-term signals.

Admission policy algorithm (high level)
- On request arrival: lookup tenant metadata in local cache.
- Compute effective weight = base_weight(tier) * contract_multiplier * dynamic_reduction_factor.
- Check local bucket for tenant: if token available -> accept and decrement.
- If bucket empty -> attempt soft-shed: if requesting tier <= standard -> return 429 with Retry-After; if gold/platinum -> attempt to steal spare capacity from lower-priority tenants (best-effort) or route to alternate region.
- If cluster-wide overload (observed queue latency > threshold): begin proportional shedding across tiers, preserving a headroom for platinum accounts.

Quota accounting and reconciliation
- Primary accounting is event-based and local for low-latency enforcement. Each node increments per-tenant counters and emits deltas to the control plane every 10-30s.
- Control plane maintains a near-real-time aggregate view and can adjust local caps by pushing policy diffs to nodes.
- For hard contractual limits (billing/committed QPS), control plane performs flow accounting and triggers enforcement when aggregate usage > commit + tolerance. Enforcement escalates: notify -> throttles -> restrict burst windows.

Noisy neighbor detection and mitigations
- Detects when tenant contribution to latency/error rises above X% of node degradation (moving window).
- Mitigations in order: reduce local bucket size, enforce stricter per-tenant concurrency, redirect to dedicated pool (if reserved), trigger control-plane migration recommendation, or apply adaptive sampling (drop lower-priority requests).
- Post-mitigation: automatic rollback after metrics normalize for a configurable cooldown.

Multi-region considerations
- Prefer local enforcement with best-effort global reconciliation. Each region enforces its own quotas to maintain tight latency SLOs.
- For global contracts we maintain a global committed QPS; control plane monitors per-region usage and can rebalance by nudging traffic via DNS or edge routing (requires collaboration with networking).
- Network partition behavior: if control plane unreachable, nodes should fall back to cached policy (last-writer-wins) and conservative limits (reduce non-platinum capacity by 20%).

Control plane APIs and config model (sketch)
- TenantPolicy { tenant_id, tier, committed_qps, burst_seconds, priority_weight, dedicated_pool_id?, region_affinity }
- NodePolicyPush: { node_id, effective_capacity, overrides: [tenant_id -> local_cap] }
- Events: usage_delta, breach_alert, noisy_neighbor_alert

Example runtime config snippet (pseudo-YAML)
- admission:
    default_bucket_window_ms: 1000
    local_bucket_capacity: 2000
    priority_weights: {platinum: 100, gold: 50, standard: 20, trial: 5}
- shedding:
    cluster_latency_threshold_ms: 250
    proportional_shed_min_percent: 5
    platinum_headroom_percent: 15

Observability & alerts
- Per-tenant metrics emitted from nodes: qps, p95_latency, token_drops, circuit_trips, rejection_reasons.
- Aggregates in control plane used for billing and SLA reports.
- Alerting rules: tenant_token_drop_rate > 1% for 3m, node_queueing_p95 > 300ms for 1m, cross-tenant_latency_contribution > 30% -> page SRE.

Customer UX and explainability
- Rejections include structured body explaining reason (overload, quota exceeded, noisy-mitigation) with a link to support SLA dashboard and recommended retry semantics.
- Monthly reports show committed vs actual usage and any mitigation events (for transparency and dispute resolution).

Rollout plan
1) Implement local bucket and admission hooks behind a feature flag.
2) Canary on dedicated infra with synthetic noisy-tenant tests.
3) Enable proportional shedding in low-traffic clusters, ramp to 50% of clusters over 4 weeks.
4) Integrate control-plane reconciliation and alerts.
5) Expose customer-facing metrics and docs.

Open questions / trade-offs
- Exact sizing of local buckets vs burst tolerance — needs workload characterization.
- How aggressively to preempt lower-tier traffic when reclaiming capacity for high-tier customers; legal/contract implications.
- Whether to provide an opt-in dedicated tenancy migration flow (cost + SLA negotiations).
- Coordination with networking for cross-region traffic steering — dependency and latency implications.

Next steps (owners)
- (Maya) run microbenchmarks for bucket sizing (target: 10k samples by 2024-09-30).
- (Ethan) prototype ingress admission hook + token bucket on a test node (target: 2024-10-15).
- (Priya) draft billing/invoice note for mitigation events and contract language (target: 2024-10-01).
- (Lena) implement noisy-neighbor detection metric and alert rules in staging (target: 2024-10-08).

Notes / references
- See ENGINF-2145 for prior design doc and traffic experiments.
- Slack thread summarizing initial decisions: #infra-tenant-throttle 2024-08-21.
- Related docs: tenant-routing-controls-architectural-sketch.json (background), org-aware-routing-playbook.json (playbook).

---
This is a working doc — expect iterations. Keep design focused on small runtime primitives + control-plane policy that can evolve without requiring heavy client changes.
